  - **Two plans on an in-app paywall (new):** a yearly plan preselected, because it has the highest lifetime value (unless yearly does not suit the business), plus a weekly or monthly one; any other plans sit behind a "view all plans" button that opens a sheet, so the base paywall stays simple [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. Both videos are the same consultant, Jonathan Parra, so this is one voice. The sheet is DC-L19-114's decision.
  - **How the paywall footer shows the price (new):** plan groups stacked or side by side, and both plans shown as a weekly amount with the real billed price as a subtitle, raised as things to test, not recommendations [S-L19-106].
  - **Anchoring (new):** break the price into weekly amounts (Tide) or compare it with things people already pay for, such as coffee or therapy (Ahead) [S-L19-104]. A high-priced lifetime plan that is not meant to sell raises perceived value and nudges people toward the annual plan; 4% of iOS apps on Mobbin offer one, usually at about twice the annual price [S-L19-111]. Moonly kept the number and changed the unit (8 a month became 8 a week), because people compare prices with each other rather than with value; subscribers who converted at the weekly price churned harder [S-L19-111].
  - **A plan recommended from the person's answers (new):** Grammarly recommends plans from its onboarding quiz and reports almost 20% more plan upgrades [S-L19-107].
  - **Enterprise as a small link:** a tiny Enterprise button on every plan instead of its own section; the creator estimates it is irrelevant to about 98% of visitors [S-L19-082].
  - **Card hierarchy:** plan name smaller and monthly price larger, because the price is what people care about [S-L19-061]. Give each plan a name and a short description, use check marks instead of bullets, list a feature the plan doesn't include, turn the button into an outline if it moves up the card, separate price and features with a light tint of the primary color instead of a divider, and write an actionable button label [S-L19-075].
  - **Honest numbers:** show the actual discount, or discounted plans look cheaper than lower tiers and the order stops making sense; show what the next plan adds that the current one lacks (Resend, Supabase) [S-L19-061]; a note under the price with the real billing terms, so people don't feel misled when they learn what they will pay [S-L19-075]. A clearer offer can matter as much as a better one: Tipstop (as heard) emphasised its trial, added a discount badge and made the offer easier to understand, and reports direct conversions almost tripled with the same offer [S-L19-104].
  - **One highlighted purchase:** the purchase call to action as one of the cards, marked with a gradient stroke [S-L19-082] (gradients are DC-L19-12's decision).
  - **Billing inside the product:** tabs for billing and usage, usage as a few small donut charts, the billing email and payment method [S-L19-061].
- **Visual effect:** A larger price and a smaller name put the eye on what people decide by [S-L19-061]; check marks and a listed missing feature make plans easy to compare [S-L19-075] [inferred for "easy to compare"]; a clear discount keeps the order readable [S-L19-061]. The five-plan picker, with discounts that were not shown, looks like a mess [S-L19-061]. Two plans with one preselected lower the load of choosing [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. A weekly amount looks smaller than the same price per year [inferred], which is why the billed total must stay visible.
- **Depends on (upstream):** the deceptive-pattern policy (DC-L13-15: hidden costs, comparison prevention, preselection), one high-emphasis action per region (DC-L13-18), number styling (Q-type-06, DC-L19-33, which also carries the weekly-price footer sample), gradients (Q-color-25, DC-L19-12), the paywall screen (DC-L19-139), where the paywall appears (DC-L19-135).
- **Affects (downstream):** PricingCard, a plan comparison table, the paywall plan footer, the "view all plans" sheet, a plan badge, the billing settings page, upgrade prompts (DC-L19-135), a monthly or yearly switch.
- **Token encoding:** none new. Prices use tabular digits (STD-visual-details-02); a price that animates on a monthly or yearly switch uses NumberFlow (STD-visual-details-59) [inferred application]. The price-area tint is a `color` alias of the primary at reduced opacity, such as `color.pricing.price-area` [inferred name].
- **Platform notes:** Web pricing pages and in-product billing tabs come from Kole Jain's videos; in-app subscription paywalls on phones now come from Mobbin's [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-111]. Apple began rejecting paywalls built on free-trial toggles in early 2026 [S-L19-104] (DC-L19-106 carries the rule for switches). Still not covered by any source: taxes, currencies, local prices, and monthly-or-yearly switches on web pages.
- **Accessibility constraints:** price and billing terms are real text at 4.5:1; a crossed-out old price also says it in words ("was $X"), because strikethrough is not announced reliably [inferred]; check marks and "not included" marks have text or accessible names, never an icon or color alone (WCAG 1.1.1, 1.4.1) [inferred]; the suggested or preselected plan is marked by more than color, such as a check or the word "Selected" [inferred]; the billed amount under a weekly price is body text, not faint fine print (DC-L19-36) [inferred].
- **Default + heuristic:** Web pricing page: three or four plans, one of them suggested; the price larger than the name; the real discount and the billing terms under the price; what the next plan adds; Enterprise as a small link on each plan (still visible, so not hidden in the deceptive-pattern sense [inferred]). In-app paywall: two plans, the one that suits the business preselected (yearly, by the source's reasoning), the rest one tap away behind "view all plans" [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. Whatever unit is shown large, the billed amount and period are always on screen. The two surfaces differ, they do not contradict: all plans stay reachable, so the two-plan paywall is disclosure, not a cap, which respects the research warning that choice overload does not justify removing options (L13 law table) [inferred]. A preselected plan is a default choice, not the pre-ticked consent box DC-L13-15 flags, provided the other plan is as easy to pick [inferred]. A lifetime anchor is a real plan people can buy, so it may stay; a unit change is a price change and is shown plainly; neither may hide the billed total (DC-L13-15, hidden costs) [inferred]. No source settles where anchoring turns into misleading framing, so that stays a human review. Evidence strength: the plan count and the 98% figure are one creator's opinion; the three-to-four ceiling matches the L13 research's suggested info lint (a plan picker with more than 3-4 tiers and no suggested marker or comparison) [inferred there too]; the two-plan paywall and yearly default are one consultant's experience; Moonly's unit change and lifetime anchor are one app's results.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-061] [S-L19-075] [S-L19-082] [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-107] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-15, DC-L13-18, the L13 choice-overload row, DC-L19-12, DC-L19-33, DC-L19-106 and DC-L19-114.
- **Maps to:**
  - New question (proposed Q-pattern-11, zoom 3, stage 23, show if the product sells plans or Q-scope-06 is `persuade`): "How should your plans be shown?" Options `plan-cards` (3-4 cards, one suggested; default on the web), `comparison-table` (a feature grid when plans differ on many features) [inferred option], `single-plan` (one price plus an Enterprise link) [inferred option], and new `paywall-two-plans` ("Two plans, one preselected, the rest behind 'View all plans'"; default when plans are sold inside a phone app) [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106].
  - Q-pattern-05: new detectable checks, "a discounted price shown without the real discount or the billing term" [inferred from S-L19-061 and S-L19-075] and "a price shown per week or per month with no billed amount and period on the same screen" [inferred from S-L19-106 and S-L19-111].
  - Visual samples: a pricing card before and after (check marks, a listed missing feature, a billing note, a tinted price area, an outline button) [S-L19-075]; a vibe-coded plan picker fixed (fewer plans, smaller names, bigger prices, the real discount, the next plan's extras) [S-L19-061]; a two-plan paywall footer with yearly preselected, beside the weekly-price variant with the billed price as a subtitle [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]; Tide's weekly breakdown and Ahead's comparison with coffee [S-L19-104].
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Plan cards:* now easy to compare. As plans or features grow, cards overflow and a comparison table takes over [inferred].
  - *Comparison table:* now thorough. It suits growing feature lists but reads as dense on phones [inferred].
  - *Single plan:* now the simplest choice. As customer types diverge, it forces an early split into tiers [inferred].
  - *Two-plan paywall:* now a quick choice. As plans are added, they go into the sheet, and the preselected plan has to be rechecked against the business [S-L19-106] [inferred].
  - *Anchors and unit changes:* now may lift conversion. Moonly's weekly payers churned harder [S-L19-111], and every price change needs the honesty check again [inferred].
  - *Honest numbers:* now a few more lines of text. They prevent support load and distrust as prices and discounts change [S-L19-075] [inferred for support load].
- **Standards:** STD-visual-details-02, STD-visual-details-59, STD-visual-details-29, STD-visual-details-31, STD-visual-details-35, STD-visual-details-44

### DC-L19-135: Paywalls, upsells and re-engagement prompts
- **Block path:** Principles > Ethics > Monetization and engagement prompts
- **Questions the designer answers:** What may sit behind a paywall or an account wall? At which moments may a paywall or upgrade prompt appear, and is it one offer or one per feature? Can people close it? What happens when someone declines, tries to cancel or is about to leave? May the product comment on how much someone uses it, keep reminding them, or punish a lapse? Can people turn intrusive features off?
- **Options:**
  - **Upgrade prompt at the limit:** show what the higher plan unlocks where the limit applies [inferred placement]; the source's hover version (after Dub) reveals the Pro limits by sliding the new limit in and the old number out, instead of crossed-out text [S-L19-079]; show what the next plan includes [S-L19-061].
  - **Touch points across the customer's life (new):** after onboarding (the most used; 78% of iOS apps on Mobbin), at a gated feature, in settings, when a subscriber tries to cancel (a win-back offer) and before the app is deleted [S-L19-106] [S-L19-104]. A well-designed paywall at the wrong moment is still a bad paywall [S-L19-104].
  - **One offer, or one paywall per feature (new):** every contextual, per-feature paywall lost Moonly's A/B tests, because people thought each feature had to be bought separately, so Moonly went back to one consistent paywall; the video then shows Orbit's paywall making clear that paying today unlocks all features [S-L19-111]. Parra says paywalls at different touch points speak more to the user because they are more personal [S-L19-104]. They fit as "many moments, one offer": show it where it is relevant, and each time say that one plan unlocks everything [inferred].
  - **Soft or hard (new):** a soft paywall can be closed and the app used; Moonly's won across its tests, though its close button appears only after 5 seconds. A hard paywall has no way past without paying; the host reports that hard paywalls won in the US [S-L19-111].
  - **Leaving and cancelling (new):** an exit-intent sheet that offers the monthly plan when someone turns down the yearly one [S-L19-104]; steep discounts kept for win-back when a subscriber tries to cancel, not straight after onboarding, where an 80%-off offer can cannibalise revenue [S-L19-106]; a longer trial instead of an aggressive last-minute discount, to stay compliant and keep trust [S-L19-104]. ClassPass takes fewer than five screens to subscribe and 17 to cancel [S-L19-104].
  - **Offers that help (new):** Moonly's AI guide recommends an add-on only when that add-on can really help the person at that moment [S-L19-111]. In a demo whose brief asked where an offers nudge belongs without feeling manipulative, the agent put it on the home page right after onboarding, citing an app that does the same [S-L19-108].
  - **A wall in front of simple content:** a recipe behind a paywall or an account requirement, presented as infuriating [S-L19-048].
  - **Pressure tactics:** a usage-shaming message whose only choices are upgrading or more of the same notifications; a progress warning with a button nudging the user to lower their goal; a streak punishment that makes a reader guess where they were; endless pop-ups and premium tiers that add nothing [S-L19-048]. That video is satire: each is presented as what makes products maddening. New, from practice: a spin-the-wheel paywall whose wheel is predetermined to land on a discount, which the consultant says works for short-term weekly revenue while more and more people learn to close paywalls and wait for an offer [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], and fake urgency, which the paywall video's narrator says people stop believing once every app uses it [S-L19-104]; a one-time offer that is gone once closed, paired with animation and haptics to pull attention [S-L19-104]; prices set by device (higher on a new phone on 5G), described without a word on fairness [S-L19-106].
  - **An off switch:** three of the deliberately annoying features in the satire (the forced layer-naming modal, the streak punishment and neighbour control of smart-home devices) come with a way to turn them off: a notice, a button beside them or a setting [S-L19-048]. The usage-shaming message does not; its only choices are upgrading or more notifications.
  - **The research policy:** DC-L13-15's enforced lint (pre-checked opt-ins, unequal accept and decline, re-prompting after a dismissal, fake countdowns, confirmshaming copy, cancelling harder than signing up).
- **Visual effect:** A prompt at the limit reads as help; a shaming or guilt prompt reads as hostile [S-L19-048]; a wall in front of simple content reads as a trap [S-L19-048] [inferred for "trap"]. One paywall that says it unlocks everything reads as one purchase; a string of per-feature paywalls reads as paying piece by piece [S-L19-111]. Fake urgency stops working once every app uses it [S-L19-104].
- **Depends on (upstream):** DC-L13-15 and Q-pattern-05 (still Planned), tone (DC-L19-37: never shame the user), pricing (DC-L19-134), the paywall screen (DC-L19-139), sheets (DC-L19-114), offer motion and haptics (DC-L19-83, DC-L19-98).
- **Affects (downstream):** upgrade banners and limit states, paywall screens, the exit-intent sheet, win-back and cancellation flows, the delete-account flow, one-time offers, notification and reminder prompts, streak and progress UI, feature toggles in settings.
- **Token encoding:** none; lint rules in `$extensions` or config (DC-L13-15).
- **Platform notes:** Apple began rejecting paywalls built on free-trial toggles in early 2026 [S-L19-104] (DC-L19-106). Moonly added Stripe beside Apple's payments in the US, partly because half of cancellations came within 3 minutes of purchase when cancelling was one tap, and reports lifetime value doubled; it advises against Google's alternative billing on Android [S-L19-111]. These are dated, market-specific reports. Where people pay (store, web or both) and what the store allows on a paywall are DC-L19-155's decision, which also proposes a Q-pattern-05 check for a free-trial toggle on an iOS paywall; this card does not repeat it. Notification permission primers are DC-L19-129's [S-L19-107].
- **Accessibility constraints:** an upgrade detail shown on hover also needs a non-hover path (STD-accessibility-motion-15) [inferred]; paywalls and prompts always have a way out (STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-visual-details-33), visible from the first frame, so a close control delayed by 5 seconds [S-L19-111] does not qualify (DC-L19-114 says the same) [inferred application]; a decline option is never low-contrast (DC-L13-15 notes visual interference overlaps with contrast failures); a haptic fired when an offer appears is an entrance the person did not cause, which STD-springs-gestures-61 forbids (DC-L19-83, DC-L19-98) [inferred application].
- **Default + heuristic:** Confirms Q-pattern-05's default `enforced`. Upgrade prompts appear at the limit, say what the next plan adds, and accept one dismissal that sticks (no re-prompting, the DSA example in DC-L13-15). Plan the paywall's moments (after onboarding, a gated feature, settings, cancel), but make every one the same offer that unlocks everything [S-L19-111] [S-L19-104] [inferred reconciliation]. Premium features may be locked, but the paywall itself always has a visible way out, from its first frame, back to whatever is free [inferred application of STD-visual-details-33 and STD-accessibility-motion-24]; so OpenDesigner does not recommend a hard paywall or a delayed close, even where one app reports that they won [S-L19-111]. Exit-intent and win-back screens count toward the cancel flow's length, which must stay no longer than sign-up (DC-L13-15's hard-to-cancel lint and the DSA example) [inferred]; ClassPass is the example to avoid [S-L19-104]. Steep discounts only for win-back, never straight after onboarding [S-L19-106]. A "one-time" offer must really be one-time; one that returns after it was said to be gone is fake scarcity [inferred mapping]. Candidate checks: (1) an engagement feature (reminder, usage nudge, streak prompt) with no off switch: warning [inferred]; (2) an upsell attached to a usage or guilt message: human review as confirmshaming [inferred mapping]; (3) a paywall or account wall in front of content promoted as free: human review; (4) a lapse that removes progress or blocks content: human review; (5) new: a cancel flow with more screens than sign-up, counting exit-intent and win-back screens: warning (DC-L13-15's own lint, now with a real example [S-L19-104]); (6) new: a paywall or offer whose close control is missing or delayed: error (STD-accessibility-motion-24) [S-L19-111]; (7) new: a prize wheel or lottery with a fixed outcome: human review as fake urgency or scarcity [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [inferred mapping]; (8) new: prices that vary by device or network: human review, since no source weighs their fairness [S-L19-106]. Evidence strength: the satire [S-L19-048] mocks pressure and the paywall consultant pushes back on it (he has a hard time accepting the prize wheel and says it may not suit a long-term business) [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], for different reasons, so two channels agree; [S-L19-104] and [S-L19-106] are one interview; the Moonly results are one app's; DC-L13-15 supplies the policy and legal anchors.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-048] [S-L19-079] [S-L19-061] [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-108] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-15, DC-L19-37, DC-L19-83, DC-L19-98, DC-L19-106, DC-L19-114 and DC-L19-155 (store rules and where people pay).
- **Maps to:**
  - Q-pattern-05: confirms `enforced`; the off-switch check is the simplest first lint to build while the question is Planned [inferred]; checks 5 and 6 are machine-detectable once a flow is described and join the enforced subset; 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 are human-review items. Suggested addition to the `enforced` label: "every paywall and offer shows its close control from the start" [inferred].
  - Q-pattern-05 visual samples: the anti-pattern gallery (the 342-videos message with an upsell, the step-goal pop-up with a button suggesting a lower goal, the streak punishment) [S-L19-048] beside an upgrade prompt that slides the higher limit in [S-L19-079]; a spin-the-wheel paywall beside a trial timeline [S-L19-104]; ClassPass as a count, under five screens to join against 17 to cancel [S-L19-104]; per-feature paywalls beside one paywall that unlocks everything [S-L19-111].
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Prompt at the limit:* now slightly less conversion pressure. It keeps trust as the user base grows [inferred].
  - *Many moments, one offer:* now one paywall to maintain. New gated features reuse it instead of adding paywalls, so the message "one plan unlocks everything" holds as features grow [S-L19-111] [inferred].
  - *Soft paywall with a visible close:* now some people leave without paying. They can still convert later; Moonly's one-time offer, usually on day three, is aimed at people for whom price was the blocker [S-L19-111].
  - *Win-back and exit offers:* now keep some people who were leaving [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. As they pile up, the cancel flow lengthens, and people learn that leaving brings a discount [S-L19-104].
  - *Walls and pressure tactics:* now more upgrades or weekly revenue, perhaps [S-L19-104]. They breed resentment, people learn to close paywalls [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], and the research notes laws moving against them (DC-L13-15).
  - *Off switch:* now one setting per feature. As engagement features multiply, a settings page of switches keeps people in control (STD-visual-details-39).
- **Standards:** STD-visual-details-39, STD-visual-details-44, STD-visual-details-45, STD-visual-details-33, STD-accessibility-motion-15, STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-springs-gestures-61

### DC-L19-136: Progress, streaks and rewards
- **Block path:** Patterns > Engagement > Progress and gamification
- **Questions the designer answers:** Does the product show progress toward the person's own goals? Does it add a streak, a currency, badges or leaderboards? If a streak, which feeling brings people back: fear of losing it, optimism, attachment to a character, or a visible chain of days? What must someone do each day to keep it, and what happens when they miss a day? What does the product prove before it asks for effort?
- **Options:**
  - **None:** the product's value is the reason to return. For everyday work tools the house standard is to remove friction rather than add delight (STD-when-to-animate-20).
  - **Progress only:** show what has been done and what is left, as Exercism shows the share of a language completed [S-L19-078]; a percentage, not "in progress" [S-L19-086]; multi-step flows show position and total (the L13 goal-gradient default).
  - **A streak, and the feeling it leans on (new):** Mobbin's review of 859 streak designs sorts them by lever [S-L19-105]. *Fear of loss:* more urgent copy, a countdown clock and a mascot that makes you feel guilty. *Optimism:* encouraging copy, a button reworded as a promise to yourself, and milestones collected as proof of progress (Opal). *Attachment:* a mascot that cheers you on or grows alongside you. *Visual attention:* days shown as a visible chain in which a gap stands out at once. The video describes the fear lever without endorsing it and asks whether streaks build habits or only make people afraid to stop [S-L19-105]. The copy is DC-L19-37's decision, the commitment button's label DC-L19-38's and DC-L19-104's, and the mascot DC-L19-77's.
  - **Flexible streak rules (new):** Duolingo's streak freeze lets people miss a day without losing everything; allowing up to two equipped at a time raised daily active learners by 0.38%, over 200,000 more people a day. A variant where one lesson keeps the streak alive beat one that required the full daily goal, with over 40% more people keeping a 7-day streak. Apps increasingly offer repairs, freezes, pauses and grace days, designing for recovery rather than perfection [S-L19-105]. The video cites an unnamed study in which missing a day had almost no effect on whether a habit became automatic [S-L19-105].
  - **The habit loop as a checklist (new):** cue (a reminder that shows the streak number, before the app is opened), craving (a short sound after each session, like Duolingo's jingle), response (make the next step easy, such as auto-advancing) and reward. Once the streak is routine the reward loses its pull, so apps add surprises such as animations, milestone celebrations and bonus XP [S-L19-105]; how much of that the house allows is DC-L19-83's decision.
  - **A game layer:** one central currency earned by the core actions (Duolingo XP, Todoist Karma) that shows progress; a streak kept alive by the core action; rewards scaled to the size of the goal; badges for milestones such as 30 days in a row; short quizzes that pay the currency. Rewards must tie to real goals, because meaningless rewards motivate no one [S-L19-078].
  - **A metric of its own (new):** a named measure people adopt in their own words: streaks (Duolingo), a readiness score (Oura), closing the rings (Apple). The video claims, without data, that people who talk in the metric rarely switch products [S-L19-110]. Recaps and highlights package the stats: Origin's weekly recap and daily brief, and Runner's post-run highlights, which give a sense of accomplishment [S-L19-110].
  - **A social layer:** leaderboards and public badges; a league with promotion, neutral and demotion zones (Duolingo); a local leaderboard when the ranking involves money, to account for income and currency differences [S-L19-078].
  - **Sharing as a reason to come back** [inferred framing]: in a yearly recap, the share button is always visible because sharing is why the recap succeeds; one share button with scopes (slide, chapter, whole recap); the owner's name on shared content; a short comparison with last year [S-L19-076]. New: Opal turns screen-time insights into a swipeable story people share [S-L19-110]; Moonly offers a ready-made one-tap share flow when someone takes a screenshot, because people share insights about themselves, not features, and reports that 23% of users share something [S-L19-111].
  - **Rejected:** punishing a broken streak [S-L19-048]; meaningless rewards [S-L19-078]; fear and guilt as the lever [S-L19-105], which DC-L19-37 rules out as tone aimed at the person; making streaks stricter after people lapse, the obvious fix that Duolingo found worked worse than flexibility [S-L19-105]. Removing choices so the core action needs no decision works for TikTok because its algorithm learns what people want [S-L19-077]; the research warns that choice overload averages near zero and does not justify deleting options (L13 choice-overload row), and lists addictive design among the patterns to watch (DC-L13-15).
- **Visual effect:** Visible progress and a single currency give a sense of momentum [S-L19-078]; leaderboards add comparison and pressure [S-L19-078] [inferred for "pressure"]; punishments make the product feel hostile [S-L19-048]. A chain of days makes a gap visible at once; urgent copy, a countdown and a guilty mascot create fear and guilt; encouraging copy and collectible milestones make progress feel like building a better self [S-L19-105].
- **Depends on (upstream):** audience and use (Q-aud-01, Q-scope-06), how lively the brand is (Q-brand-04), the deceptive-pattern policy (DC-L13-15), tone (DC-L19-37), the mascot (DC-L19-77, Q-img-04), the commitment button label (DC-L19-104), sound (Q-motion-08), onboarding order (DC-L19-129: value before the game).
- **Affects (downstream):** progress bar or ring, streak counter, a day chain or calendar, streak freeze, repair and grace-day controls, badge, leaderboard, currency counter, recap and highlights, share sheet, milestone celebrations (DC-L19-130), reminder notifications and their settings, glance views (Q-pattern-06) [inferred].
- **Token encoding:** none new. Counters use tabular digits (STD-visual-details-02) and animate with NumberFlow (STD-visual-details-59); celebrations use the expressive motion set (DC-L04-19).
- **Platform notes:** a milestone may get one success haptic, never one per frame or on scroll (STD-springs-gestures-61). A reminder that shows the streak number is the cue before the app is opened [S-L19-105]; a streak or goal is a candidate for a widget or complication (Q-pattern-06) [inferred]. A completion sound fits Q-motion-08's `rare-events` option, behind mute, and never as the only signal (STD-springs-gestures-61, STD-accessibility-motion-20) [inferred].
- **Accessibility constraints:** progress rings and bars show the value in text; a day chain also says it in words ("5 of 7 days") rather than by filled color alone [inferred]; league zones are not marked by color alone; celebrations respect reduced motion (STD-accessibility-motion-02); nothing is lost to a time limit the person cannot extend (WCAG 2.2.1) [inferred], which freezes and grace days help with [inferred link].
- **Default + heuristic:** `none` for work tools; `progress` for products built around the person's own goals; a streak or a game or social layer only with an explicit goal, and then with these conditions: optimism or a visible chain as the lever, never fear or guilt [S-L19-105] (DC-L19-37); one unit of the core action keeps the streak alive; freezes, repairs or grace days built in [S-L19-105]; the milestone is celebrated and the daily completion only confirmed (DC-L19-83); rewards tie to real goals and value is shown before any game [S-L19-078]; reminders and other engagement features have an off switch [inferred, generalising the three off switches in S-L19-048]; progress is honest, with no artificial head start (the L13 goal-gradient ethics note). The rule that a missed day is never punished rested on satire [S-L19-048]; Duolingo's reported results now back it [S-L19-105], so two channels agree. Judge a streak by whether people come back after a break and reach their goal, not by daily engagement alone, because the video warns that engagement is not the same as a lasting habit [S-L19-105] (DC-L19-137). Differs from [S-L19-105] on one point: it explains the visible chain with the Zeigarnik effect, which the L13 research marks as a failed replication. The chain can stay, because people do tend to resume unfinished tasks (the Ovsiankina tendency in the L13 table), but no reminder or nag may be justified by Zeigarnik (the L13 "no nag" rule). The Duolingo figures come from the video without a linked study; the claim that a coined metric stops people switching has no data [S-L19-110].
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-078] [S-L19-086] [S-L19-076] [S-L19-048] [S-L19-077] [S-L19-105] [S-L19-110] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-15, the L13 goal-gradient, peak-end, choice-overload and Zeigarnik rows, DC-L19-37, DC-L19-77, DC-L19-83 and DC-L19-104.
- **Maps to:**
  - New question (proposed Q-pattern-12, zoom 3, stage 23, show if Q-aud-01 is `regular` or `large`): "Should the product use progress, streaks or rewards to bring people back?" Options `none` (default when Q-scope-06 is `operate`), `progress` (default otherwise), new `streak` ("a streak kept by one unit of the core action, with freezes or grace days") [S-L19-105], `game-layer`, `social` [inferred defaults].
  - Q-pattern-12 heuristic (new): "A streak never punishes a missed day and never leans on fear or guilt; celebrate the milestone, confirm the day" [S-L19-105] [S-L19-048]; the last clause is DC-L19-83's rule, not the video's [inferred].
  - Q-pattern-05: fear-based streak screens (countdowns, guilt) are a human-review item; a lint cannot catch them, because a streak's end-of-day deadline is real [inferred].
  - Visual samples: a fear-based streak screen beside an optimism-based one [S-L19-105]; a streak freeze and a day chain with one gap [S-L19-105]; the savings app's goal home, league leaderboard with promotion and demotion zones, and analytics with overspending marked [S-L19-078]; the recap with one share button and three scopes [S-L19-076]; Opal's story-format insights [S-L19-110].
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *None:* now nothing to maintain. Return visits depend entirely on the product's value.
  - *Progress:* now one bar per goal. It stays honest and cheap as goals multiply [inferred].
  - *Flexible streak:* now a daily cue and a few rules (freeze, repair, grace day). The longer a streak runs, the more it becomes part of people's identity, which is why losing one makes some people quit [S-L19-105]; recovery rules keep them coming back.
  - *Game layer:* now motivating. Every new feature must be priced in the currency, and the economy needs balancing as it grows [inferred].
  - *Metric of its own:* now a name to define and explain. It becomes vocabulary the product must keep stable as features change [inferred].
  - *Social layer:* now adds comparison. As users grow, fairness (local boards, leagues) and moderation become work [S-L19-078] [inferred for moderation].
  - *Sharing:* now one share control. Each shared item carries the brand to new people [S-L19-076] [S-L19-111] [inferred for the brand].
- **Standards:** STD-when-to-animate-04, STD-when-to-animate-09, STD-when-to-animate-20, STD-springs-gestures-61, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-accessibility-motion-20, STD-visual-details-02, STD-visual-details-59, STD-visual-details-39, STD-visual-details-44, STD-visual-details-45, STD-visual-details-47

### DC-L19-137: Measuring whether a design change worked
- **Block path:** Process > Measurement > Product outcomes
- **Questions the designer answers:** What is this page or flow for: sales, sign-ups, enquiries, subscriptions? Which number should the change move, and which number must not get worse? How will we check it: analytics before and after, an A/B test, or a usability test? What gets tested first? Who can see the analytics?
- **Options:**
  - **Not measured:** the page is judged on looks. The source says clients mostly judge looks while users care whether it works, and a site that looks good but serves no purpose still won't sell [S-L19-038]. An ugly, text-heavy paywall beat every polished design for one app [S-L19-104], so looks alone do not predict results.
  - **Before and after:** compare the site's analytics before and after the new design ships; build the site yourself or keep view-only access so you can [S-L19-038]. Weaker than a controlled test, because other things change over time [inferred].
  - **Controlled A/B test:** when you build option A and option B, validate them and ship the winner, not both (STD-when-to-animate-22); break a familiar pattern only with proof, and test rather than assume (STD-visual-details-37). A/B tests and analytics need large traffic (L13 methods table). New, from practice: keep the current screen as the control and test four to five new designs against it; some wins needed a second or third experiment to become statistically significant [S-L19-106]. Moonly runs hundreds of tests a month, uses AI tools to reconcile its analytics and recommend ship, don't ship or collect more data, and reports its paywall going from 10% conversion in 2020 to 40% on paid traffic through small, almost daily tests in which every element had to win its place [S-L19-111].
  - **Usability testing only:** about five people per round finds most problems (L13 methods table), but the samples of small pre-launch tests are too small to prove impact [S-L19-038].
  - **A main number plus a guard number (new):** pick the main number by the kind of business: ARPU for an app built to launch fast and gather users, LTV and retention for a long-term business, because weekly plans can show a $3-4 ARPU while monthly churn runs at 90-95% [S-L19-106]. For a paywall the consultant also watches the share of installs that reach the paywall (above 80% is good, 90% or more excellent), trial-to-paid conversion, day-1, day-7 and day-30 retention, and churn [S-L19-106]. Retention and LTV matter more than the first payment [S-L19-104], and engagement is not the same as a lasting habit [S-L19-105].
  - **What to test first (new):** radically different designs first (a video, a bullet list, a trial timeline, a long-form page), then personalisation, then how plans and prices are packaged, with device-based pricing last because it is the most work for the smallest gain [S-L19-106] [S-L19-104]. Moonly's founder calls pricing tests the most important and images the biggest lever [S-L19-111]. The two run different products, and both say to test rather than assume.
  - **Validate the market first (new):** a lean web funnel before building the full app, for fast signals at low cost [S-L19-111].
  - **Where to spend effort:** for a site with heavy traffic, conversion rate optimisation beats more SEO, because a small gain at that scale is worth a lot [S-L19-038].
  - **Reporting:** short case studies with the services, the problem, and the solution with numbers [S-L19-038].
- **Visual effect:** none on screen (a process decision). Recorded metrics sit next to the decisions they belong to, so later sessions know what each change was for [inferred].
- **Depends on (upstream):** what the screens are for (Q-scope-06), the system-level success measures (Q-gov-05, DC-L11-20), which measure adoption of the design system rather than product outcomes, DC-L19-166, which proposes product results before and after as one way to judge the whole system, and the paywall and onboarding decisions whose results are measured (DC-L19-139, DC-L19-129, DC-L19-136).
- **Affects (downstream):** `opendesigner/decisions.md` entries, DESIGN.md, the deceptive-pattern policy (conversion pressure is where DC-L13-15 gets tested), A/B variant prototypes.
- **Token encoding:** none (process). A decision can carry `expected_effect { metric, guard_metric, baseline, check: "before-after" | "ab-test" | "usability" }`, mirroring DC-L11-20's `metrics[]` shape [inferred].
- **Platform notes:** most website builders include basic analytics [S-L19-038]; the paywall metrics above come from consumer phone apps [S-L19-106] [S-L19-111]. App-store analytics tools are not covered by any source.
- **Accessibility constraints:** no variant may drop below the floors to win a test: both A and B pass WCAG 2.2 AA contrast, 24 px targets, visible focus and reduced motion [inferred]; a trick that raises conversion is still a deceptive pattern (DC-L13-15): the paywall consultant says a spin-the-wheel offer works for short-term weekly revenue but may not suit a long-term business [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106], and the paywall video's narrator adds that people stop believing fake urgency once every app uses it [S-L19-104].
- **Default + heuristic:** For `persuade` screens and paywalls, record the one number each major change is meant to move, plus one guard number that must not get worse (retention or churn next to a conversion number) [S-L19-106] [S-L19-105] [inferred proposal]; check it before and after at minimum; run a controlled test only with enough traffic, test big differences before details, and ship the winner (STD-when-to-animate-22); never claim impact from a five-person test. The first version of this card rested on one freelancer's video [S-L19-038]; the practice of testing against a control now also comes from a paywall consultant [S-L19-106] and an app founder [S-L19-111] on another channel, backed by two house standards and the L13 methods table. The consultant's percentages and "four to five variants" are one practitioner's habits, not thresholds. No research card covers product experiments (DC-L11-20 measures the system). DC-L19-166 uses the same kind of evidence for a system-level check; this card works per change.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-038] [S-L19-104] [S-L19-105] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L11-20, DC-L13-15, DC-L19-166 and the L13 Part D methods table.
- **Maps to:**
  - New question (proposed Q-pattern-13, zoom 3, show if Q-scope-06 is `persuade` or the product sells plans): "Which number should this page move, and how will you check it?" Options `not-measured`, `before-after` (default), `ab-test`, `usability-only`. The answer is saved with the decision, together with two new fields: the guard number, and the kind of business (quick launch or long-term), which decides the main number [S-L19-106].
  - Q-pattern-13 heuristic (new): "Test big differences before details; judge a win by the main number and the guard number together" [S-L19-106] [S-L19-105].
  - Q-gov-05: new note, "DC-L19-166's `outcomes` option judges the system by product results before and after; the per-change numbers recorded by Q-pattern-13 feed it".
  - Visual samples: a short case-study card with services, problem, and solution with numbers [S-L19-038]; a paywall experiment laid out as the control plus four to five variants [S-L19-106] [inferred layout].
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Not measured:* now no setup. Design arguments stay matters of taste as the team grows [inferred].
  - *Before and after:* now needs analytics access. It gives a rough signal that gets noisier as more changes ship at once [inferred].
  - *A/B test:* now needs traffic and tooling. It scales best, because each change is judged on its own (STD-when-to-animate-22); at Moonly's pace it also needs help reconciling the numbers [S-L19-111].
  - *Usability only:* now cheap and fast for finding problems. It never proves impact, however many rounds are run [S-L19-038].
  - *Main number plus guard:* now one more number to watch. As tests pile up, it stops wins that lift conversion while churn rises [S-L19-106] [inferred].
- **Standards:** STD-when-to-animate-22, STD-visual-details-37, STD-visual-details-44

### DC-L19-138: AI workspace components beyond labels
- **Block path:** Patterns > AI > Workspace components
- **Questions the designer answers:** If the product generates content, does it keep a searchable history? If the AI remembers things, can people see and edit that memory? Can people edit part of a response in place? What shows while the AI works? Are confidence levels shown? Can people ask the AI why a number on a dashboard changed? Does an AI product need onboarding at all?
- **Options:** (all from one Kole Jain video [S-L19-055] unless noted)
  - **A prompt box as the front door:** a large prompt box above the fold gets people trying the tool at once; ChatGPT and Gemini dropped their landing pages. A useful box previews attached PDFs and images, compresses long pasted code into a block, offers context chips that change the mode, integration buttons, and progressive disclosure such as an advanced toggle or a cost estimate above the input.
  - **Generation history:** called essential when the product outputs text, code or images; organised by session or tied to the source block, with a first-line preview, deletion, and search, which turns history into a workspace.
  - **Memory panel:** if the AI has persistent memory, it must be visible and under the user's control: see storage, bulk delete, add facts. The source criticises tools that hide it in settings.
  - **Inline editing:** highlight any part of a response and type the change (Claude, Lex, Notion AI).
  - **While it works:** short, looping, fluid loaders; streamed output; skeletons with shimmer; a trail of steps (documents retrieved, sources cited) fading in one by one (see DC-L19-127).
  - **Confidence indicator:** a pill under each response ("high confidence", "unverified"), clickable for the number.
  - **A dark "soft glass" look:** a style trend, not a pattern; it falls under the house rules for translucency.
  - **AI that explains the data (new):** people staring at a dashboard ask why a number changed; AI fills that gap as a single prompt right below a chart or a full AI layer beside the data. AI dashboards get about twice the saves and exports of the average dashboard screen on Mobbin, which shows what designers collect, not what users prefer [S-L19-110].
  - **Little or no onboarding (new):** for AI chat the first prompt is where people find value, so letting them in fast may be best; only 7% of AI apps personalise during onboarding, letting the product learn from use instead [S-L19-107] (DC-L19-129).
  - **Offers from the assistant (new):** Moonly's AI guide recommends a paid add-on only when that add-on can really help the person at that moment [S-L19-111] (DC-L19-135). How the assistant looks is DC-L19-78's decision.
- **Visual effect:** History and memory make the tool feel like a workspace; inline edits feel like revising, not regenerating; a step trail makes the AI feel like a collaborator rather than a black box; streaming turns delay into anticipation [S-L19-055].
- **Depends on (upstream):** Q-ai-01 (whether and how AI appears), DC-L13-16 (AI interface patterns), DC-L08-22 (AI module), wait feedback (DC-L19-127), dashboard charts (DC-L19-122), onboarding (DC-L19-129).
- **Affects (downstream):** prompt input, attachment chip, context chips, history list with search, memory panel, inline-edit popover, streaming text container, skeleton, step trail, confidence badge, an "ask about this chart" prompt.
- **Token encoding:** existing AI roles (`color.ai.*`, `icon.ai`) and thinking-indicator motion from DC-L13-16; nothing new [inferred].
- **Platform notes:** the examples are web and desktop AI tools; no source covers native mobile AI patterns.
- **Accessibility constraints:** streamed text must not flood screen readers, and the view must not autoscroll to the end (DC-L13-16); the step trail and confidence level are text, not color alone; glass surfaces become frostier or solid under reduced transparency (STD-accessibility-motion-11), and text on them gets higher contrast (STD-visual-details-13); memory and history deletion are undoable or confirmed, as with any destructive action (STD-visual-details-40).
- **Default + heuristic:** For products whose Q-ai-01 answer is `chat` or `presence-mode`: a prompt box with attachment previews, searchable history, streamed output, and the stop, regenerate, edit and copy controls DC-L13-16 already asks for. A memory panel is required whenever the AI keeps memory [S-L19-055]; this fits the house rule to add previews, confirmations and disclaimers to AI features (STD-visual-details-45) [inferred link]. Two points differ from the source and follow DC-L13-16: a step trail may show retrieval steps and citations, but not narrated reasoning presented as an explanation; and confidence labels belong in high-stakes contexts, not under every response. For data products, a prompt under charts that answers "why did this change?" is worth offering [S-L19-110], and its answer names the data and period it used, with no narrated reasoning presented as explanation (DC-L13-16) [inferred application]. An AI chat product can skip onboarding when the first prompt is the value (DC-L19-129) [S-L19-107]. The workspace parts are one creator's survey of current tools [S-L19-055]; the dashboard AI trend is one Mobbin presenter's observation [S-L19-110].
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-055] [S-L19-107] [S-L19-110] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-16, DC-L08-22, DC-L19-78, DC-L19-122, DC-L19-127, DC-L19-129 and DC-L19-135.
- **Maps to:**
  - Q-ai-01: new follow-up (zoom 3, show if Q-ai-01 is not `none`), multi-select "Which AI workspace parts does the product need?": `history`, `memory-panel`, `inline-edit`, `step-trail`, `confidence`, and new `explain-data` ("a prompt under charts that answers why a number changed") [S-L19-110]; default `history` for `chat`, and `explain-data` when Q-layout-03 is `data` [inferred].
  - Q-ai-01: new heuristic, "memory that exists is shown and editable". New heuristic: "an AI answer about data names the data and period it used" [inferred from S-L19-110 and DC-L13-16].
  - Visual samples: a prompt box with attachment previews and context chips; a research trail fading in step by step; a confidence pill under an answer [S-L19-055].
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Prompt box and history:* now the core of the product. Search keeps history useful as generations pile up [S-L19-055].
  - *Memory panel:* now one more screen. As memory grows, people need bulk delete and storage limits to stay in control [S-L19-055].
  - *Inline edit:* now faster fixes. Each new output type (code, images) needs its own way to select a part [inferred].
  - *Step trail and confidence:* now more trust. They have to stay honest as models change, or they mislead (DC-L13-16).
  - *Explain the data:* now a prompt under charts. As data sources multiply, each answer must say what it used, or it misleads [inferred].
- **Standards:** STD-visual-details-45, STD-visual-details-40, STD-accessibility-motion-11, STD-visual-details-13, STD-accessibility-motion-02

### DC-L19-139: The subscription paywall screen: format, trial and reassurance
- **Block path:** Patterns > Commerce > Subscription paywall
- **Questions the designer answers:** What does the person see just before the paywall? Does the paywall show everything on one screen or unfold over several? What on the screen lowers the fear of paying: a trial timeline, a cancel line, reviews? Is there a free trial, how long, on which plan, and does starting it need card details? How plain or polished is the first version, and what gets tested first?
- **Options:**
  - **A plain first paywall:** a headline describing the product, a couple of bullet points on what it does, and a continue button. At the start, getting people into the app matters more than optimising [S-L19-106]; keep the base paywall simple and measure how it performs before optimising placements [S-L19-104].
  - **Outcome first, then the offer (a flow, not a screen):** sell the outcome before asking for money. Opal shows people how many years of their life they could get back and reports trial sign-ups rising from 7% to 17% [S-L19-104]. At the end of onboarding, the paywall says the person's plan is ready and speaks to the outcome they want, so it finishes onboarding instead of interrupting it [S-L19-104]; some apps put a page of social proof, or a plan with a goal date, just before it [S-L19-107]. The words are DC-L19-36's decision.
  - **Multi-page paywall:** the information unfolds over several steps, giving time to process the decision (Ahead); Parra says multi-page paywalls almost always beat single-page ones [S-L19-104].
  - **Formats to test against each other:** a bullet list, a video of the app in action with a short bullet list and simple social proof, a trial timeline, a long-form page [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]; a table showing what people miss without subscribing, which the consultant is a big fan of, though he finds tables harder to build in the paywall tool he uses (Superwall) [S-L19-104]; a "pay ramp" with no traditional paywall, one action such as "redeem your free week" (Slopes reports 25% more trial starts) [S-L19-104]. An ugly, compact, text-heavy squeeze page beat every design the consultant tried for one app, so there is no universal best paywall, only better experiments [S-L19-104].
  - **Lowering the fear of paying:** a step-by-step timeline of the free trial (Blinkist, after users felt tricked into being charged: more trial sign-ups, fewer complaints, and more push-notification opt-ins, since the reminder comes before the trial ends) [S-L19-104]; the "no commitment, cancel anytime" line under the button [S-L19-104] (DC-L19-36 owns its wording and its truth test); a longer trial rather than an aggressive last-minute discount, which the consultant prefers to stay compliant [S-L19-104]; trial length is itself a test: Headspace's 14-day trial on the annual plan beat both its 7-day and its 30-day trials, so longer did not always win [S-L19-104]; social proof from real reviews and ratings [S-L19-104] [S-L19-111].
  - **Trial choices (owner inputs):** a free trial [S-L19-104]; a trial only on the annual plan (Moonly at one point; no result given) [S-L19-104]; card details required to start the trial (Outsider: sign-ups fell by more than half, the conversion rate rose five times, paying customers more than doubled) [S-L19-104]; no trial, with a one-time offer later, usually on day three (Moonly: trial users got the most valuable feature free and felt they had 90% of the value; the offer lifted day-3 to day-30 revenue by about 15%). 59% of iOS paywall screens on Mobbin offer no free trial [S-L19-111].
  - **Personalised paywall:** after the design itself, personalisation moves results most: the person's name, their goals, and imagery that reflects them [S-L19-106]; plans recommended from quiz answers (Grammarly) [S-L19-107]. Imagery is DC-L19-79's and DC-L19-75's decision; the recommended plan is DC-L19-134's.
  - **Polish as the difference:** animation, custom characters and world building (Focus Town) as the level of polish the consultant expects from the most successful apps [S-L19-104]; a one-time offer shaped like a flight ticket (Focus Flight) [S-L19-107]. How much motion is DC-L19-83's decision.
  - **Rejected on iOS:** paywalls built around free-trial toggles, which Apple began rejecting in early 2026 as confusing or misleading [S-L19-104] (DC-L19-106 carries the switch rule, and DC-L19-155 the store rules and a lint check for it).
- **Visual effect:** Selling the outcome first makes the paywall feel like the natural next step rather than a wall [S-L19-104]. A multi-page paywall gives people time to take the decision in [S-L19-104]. A trial timeline answers "will I forget to cancel?" with visible dates [S-L19-104] [inferred phrasing]. A table shows what is missing without the plan, and a video shows value faster than screenshots or bullets [S-L19-104]. A plain paywall looks less crafted but can convert as well or better [S-L19-104].
- **Depends on (upstream):** whether the product sells a subscription inside the app; onboarding (DC-L19-129: 78% of iOS apps on Mobbin show the paywall right after onboarding [S-L19-106]); where the paywall appears and whether it can be closed (DC-L19-135); plans and prices (DC-L19-134); copy (DC-L19-36); imagery (DC-L19-72, DC-L19-79); the deceptive-pattern policy (Q-pattern-05, DC-L13-15); measurement (DC-L19-137).
- **Affects (downstream):** a paywall template in single-page and multi-page forms, a trial timeline (a stepper with dates), the plan footer, the reassurance line under the button (DC-L19-36's `button.subtitle` slot), a reviews and rating block, a comparison table, a video block, a pay-ramp screen, the reminder notification before a trial ends, the card-entry step.
- **Token encoding:** none new (a pattern). The trial timeline reuses the Stepper; prices use tabular digits (STD-visual-details-02). The chosen format and trial terms can be recorded as builder metadata, `$extensions.builder.paywall = { format, trial: { days, plan, cardRequired }, reassurance: [] }` [inferred].
- **Platform notes:** every example is a consumer phone app, mostly on iOS. Apple's early-2026 rejection of free-trial toggles is dated App Review behaviour [S-L19-104]. Moonly reports that, with Apple's payments, half of cancellations came within 3 minutes of purchase, and that adding Stripe in the US doubled lifetime value [S-L19-111] (market-specific and dated; where people pay and the store's paywall rules are DC-L19-155's decision, the ethics side DC-L19-135's). Web onboarding in Mobbin's sample is 21% shorter than iOS, which the video suggests may be because phones carry more permission and paywall screens [S-L19-107]. Web pricing pages are DC-L19-134's.
- **Accessibility constraints:** the paywall has a visible way out from its first frame (STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-visual-details-33; DC-L19-135). Trial dates, the billed price and the cancel terms are real text at body contrast, not faint fine print (DC-L19-36) [inferred]. A trial timeline reads as a list in text, not only as a graphic [inferred]. A video paywall has captions and no sound until asked [inferred]; motion has its reduced-motion version (STD-accessibility-motion-02). Card details are asked for at the moment they are needed, with the reason and the date of the first charge (STD-visual-details-41) [inferred application].
- **Default + heuristic:** For a product that sells a subscription inside its app: show the outcome before the paywall; start with a simple base paywall (a headline, a few bullets, one continue button); add the reassurance line only when the cancel flow is really that easy (DC-L19-36, DC-L13-15); with a trial, show a timeline with the day of the reminder and the day of the first charge; then test radically different formats against that base before testing details [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106]. Trial terms are owner inputs: the interview records them and never invents them (AGENTS.md). Heuristic: "Would this person be surprised by the charge?" If yes, add the timeline and the reminder [inferred from the Blinkist case in S-L19-104]. A trial pays when it does not give the main value away [S-L19-111] [inferred generalisation]. Evidence strength: [S-L19-104] and [S-L19-106] are one interview with the same consultant, so "multi-page almost always wins", the format list and the trial advice are one practitioner's experience, and the default does not force a multi-page paywall; [S-L19-111] is a second practitioner (an app founder) who also replays a clip of the consultant; [S-L19-107] is Mobbin's library review. Every figure (Opal, Blinkist, Slopes, Outsider, Headspace, Moonly) is one company's self-reported result without test details. No research card covers paywalls. DC-L19-134 said no source covered mobile paywalls or free trials; these sources now do, and this card holds that decision. The advice to test and then ship the winner agrees with STD-visual-details-37 and STD-when-to-animate-22.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106] [S-L19-107] [S-L19-111]. Compared against DC-L13-15, DC-L19-36, DC-L19-75, DC-L19-79, DC-L19-83, DC-L19-106, DC-L19-129, DC-L19-134, DC-L19-135, DC-L19-137 and DC-L19-155.
- **Maps to:**
  - New question (proposed Q-pattern-14, zoom 3, stage 23, show if the product sells plans and Q-plat-01 includes `ios` or `android` [inferred condition]): "How should the paywall ask for money?" Options `simple` ("A headline, a few bullets and one button; test from there"; default) [S-L19-106], `multi-page` ("Outcome first, then the offer over a few steps") [S-L19-104], `trial-timeline` ("A timeline of the trial with the reminder and charge dates"; recommended whenever there is a trial) [S-L19-104], `table` ("What you get against what you miss") [S-L19-104], `video` ("The app in action, a few bullets and reviews") [S-L19-104], `pay-ramp` ("One action such as 'redeem your free week'") [S-L19-104]. Heuristic: "There is no best paywall, only better experiments: test radically different formats before details" [S-L19-104] [S-L19-106].
  - The same question records the trial terms as owner inputs (none, days, plan, card required), set by `chosen`, not recommended [inferred].
  - Q-pattern-05: the paywall is where the enforced policy is tested most; its checks are DC-L19-135's.
  - Visual samples: Opal's outcome screen followed by its paywall [S-L19-104]; Blinkist's trial timeline [S-L19-104]; a paywall button with the reassurance line [S-L19-104]; the table and video formats [S-L19-104]; Slopes' one-button pay ramp [S-L19-104]; Focus Flight's ticket-shaped offer [S-L19-107].
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Simple paywall:* now fast to ship and easy to read. As the product grows, it becomes the control that every later test is judged against [S-L19-106].
  - *Outcome first and multi-page:* now more screens to design. Each new feature or plan change means updating the outcome story those screens tell [inferred].
  - *Trial timeline:* now one more component and a reminder notification. It cuts "I was tricked" complaints [S-L19-104] and keeps the trial honest as prices and terms change [inferred].
  - *Table:* now shows what the plan adds. The rows grow with features and need pruning [inferred].
  - *Video:* now shows value fast. Every UI change dates the video [inferred].
  - *Pay ramp:* now the least friction to start [S-L19-104]. The billed terms still have to appear before any charge, so they move to a later screen rather than disappear [inferred].
  - *Free trial:* now lowers the risk of paying [S-L19-104]. Moonly says starting a purchase and cancelling it within seconds is now a very common pattern, and its trial gave away most of the value [S-L19-111], so the trial needs rechecking as the product's main value changes [inferred].
  - *Card required or no trial:* now fewer but more serious sign-ups [S-L19-104] [S-L19-111]. People who stop at the price need another path, such as Moonly's day-3 one-time offer [S-L19-111].
- **Standards:** STD-visual-details-41, STD-visual-details-33, STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-visual-details-37, STD-when-to-animate-22, STD-visual-details-02, STD-visual-details-35, STD-visual-details-44

### DC-L19-141: Accessibility floor: WCAG 2.2 AA plus the locked house rules
- **Block path:** Foundations > Accessibility > Conformance target
- **Questions the designer answers:** Which WCAG level do we commit to? Which rules above AA are already locked, whatever we pick? What would "stricter" still add?
- **Options:**
  - **WCAG 2.2 AA plus the house locks** (the current default `wcag22-aa`, reworded): AA contrast and the 24px web target floor (guardrails), plus rules the house standards make "must" at every level. Touch targets are 44x44pt on iOS, 48dp on Android, and small web controls get a 44px hit area for touch [S-L19-016] [S-L19-004]. Pinch zoom is never disabled; inputs stay at 16px or more instead [S-L19-028]. Every animation ships its reduced-motion version, gentler rather than zero [S-L19-016] [S-L19-020]. Reduced transparency and increased contrast are handled as separate signals [S-L19-020]. Layout scales with the user's text size [S-L19-020] [S-L19-016]. Hover styles are gated to fine pointers and touch gets its own press state [S-L19-028], and a haptic is never the only feedback [S-L19-016]. Overlays sit on accessible primitives [S-L19-029] [S-L19-005] and can always be dismissed (STD-accessibility-motion-24; Vaul's non-dismissible drawer shows the failure [S-L19-097]). Visible focus is already a locked guardrail (a 2px ring at a 2px offset, `guardrails.md`); the sources add an example of making focus states more distinct (animations.dev's changelog [S-L19-001]) and use the same 2px outline at a 2px offset [S-L19-030]. A visual-only duplicate layer (a clip-path copy of a tab row or a label) is hidden from assistive technology with `aria-hidden` on its container and `tabIndex={-1}` on its buttons, and production tabs sit on an accessible Tabs primitive [S-L19-010] (STD-accessibility-motion-17). An icon placed on a photo gets a circle behind it so its contrast holds whatever the image [S-L19-054] (text and controls over images belong to DC-L19-74). The review catalog restates two locks: reduced motion keeps opacity and color and drops movement, and hover motion is gated to fine pointers [S-L19-033].
  - **AA plus stricter rules** (`wcag22-aa-plus`, reworded): what is left once touch targets are locked: 7:1 body text and fewer mid-tone text colors (DC-L01-22), and 44px targets for mouse as well as touch (WCAG 2.5.5, AAA) [inferred]. The 44px touch target in the default is already the AAA size for touch [inferred]. Kole Jain's contrast work checks colored cards and a brand color that fails with white text against WCAG without naming a level [S-L19-051], and fixes low-contrast chips without naming a standard [S-L19-086]; it fits AA and adds nothing AAA-specific [inferred].
  - **Level A only** (`wcag22-a`): offered today, but it contradicts the locked floor in AGENTS.md and `guardrails.md`, and `engine.py` already maps it to AA ("AA stays the floor"). The option promises something the system will not do.
- **Visual effect:** AA plus locks: roomy hit areas on touch, a visible focus ring, motion that fades instead of sliding for people who ask, glass that turns solid when transparency is reduced. AA plus stricter: darker secondary text, fewer light grays, a flatter and plainer look [inferred]. Level A: nothing different from AA, because the engine ignores it.
- **Depends on (upstream):** Q-aud-01 (who uses it), Q-aud-02 (what is at stake), Q-plat-01 and Q-plat-02 (which platform rules apply).
- **Affects (downstream):** `size.target.*`, the contrast validator target (`raw.contrastTarget`), focus ring tokens, the reduced-motion and reduced-transparency modes, input text size, `guardrails.md` and DESIGN.md's accessibility section.
- **Token encoding:** existing `size.target.pointer` and `size.target.touch` ($type dimension). The level itself is a validator setting (`raw.contrastTarget` AA or AAA), not a token.
- **Platform notes:** web: 24px pointer targets and 44px touch hit areas built with a pseudo-element [S-L19-004]; iOS 44pt with `hitSlop` when the visual is smaller [S-L19-016]; Android 48dp. Zoom and the 16px input rule are web-only (iOS Safari zooms smaller inputs) [S-L19-028]. In React Native, `allowFontScaling` is on by default, so a height measured at the default text size is wrong at 200% and no animation may target a hardcoded height [S-L19-016].
- **Accessibility constraints:** WCAG 2.2 AA is the locked floor; 2.5.8 (24px), 2.5.5 (44px, AAA), 1.4.4 (resize text).
- **Default + heuristic:** Default `wcag22-aa`, presented as "AA plus the house locks". Offer `wcag22-aa-plus` for money, health and government products [inferred]. Nothing below AA. Rule of thumb: the level question only decides how strict contrast and mouse targets are; touch targets, zoom, motion, transparency, contrast signals and text scaling are not up for choice.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-001] [S-L19-004] [S-L19-005] [S-L19-010] [S-L19-016] [S-L19-020] [S-L19-028] [S-L19-029] [S-L19-030] [S-L19-033] [S-L19-051] [S-L19-054] [S-L19-086] [S-L19-097]; compared with DC-L11-19, DC-L01-22, DC-L03-12, DC-L10-15, DC-L19-74.
- **Maps to:**
  - Q-aud-03: remove option `wcag22-a`, or show it as unavailable with the reason "AA is the locked floor", because `engine.py` maps it to AA and AGENTS.md locks AA.
  - Q-aud-03: `wcag22-aa` label becomes "WCAG 2.2 AA, with locked rules for touch targets, zoom, motion and text size" (confirms current default); `wcag22-aa-plus` label becomes "AA plus 7:1 body text and 44px targets for the mouse too" (the "bigger targets" wording is already true for touch).
  - Q-aud-03 new heuristic [inferred]: when Q-aud-02 is `high-trust`, pre-select `wcag22-aa-plus` as the recommendation.
  - Visual sample: the Show strip lists each locked rule with its standard id, for example "Touch targets 44pt / 48dp (STD-mobile-touch-09)".
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *AA plus locks:* now, a little extra layout room for hit areas and one extra CSS block per animation. As it grows, components carry the locks, so new screens inherit them; the risk is a hand-rolled component that skips them, which review catches.
  - *AA plus stricter:* now, a narrower, darker palette. As it grows, every new text color, theme and brand color must pass 7:1, which gets harder with each addition.
  - *Level A:* now, no effect (mapped to AA). As it grows, it only misleads the person who picked it.
- **Standards:** STD-mobile-touch-09, STD-mobile-touch-11, STD-accessibility-motion-01, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-accessibility-motion-11, STD-accessibility-motion-12, STD-accessibility-motion-13, STD-accessibility-motion-15, STD-accessibility-motion-16, STD-accessibility-motion-17, STD-accessibility-motion-20, STD-accessibility-motion-24, STD-accessibility-motion-27

### DC-L19-142: Device settings the product always follows, and controls inside the app
- **Block path:** Foundations > Accessibility > User settings > Device signals and in-app controls
- **Questions the designer answers:** Which device settings does the product obey without being asked? Which extra controls, if any, live inside the app? Can people rearrange or hide parts of the interface?
- **Options:**
  - **Follow every device signal (always on, not a choice):** reduced motion, reduced transparency and increased contrast as three separate signals, and the user's text size, all built into components [S-L19-020]; in React Native, `useReducedMotion()` or `reduceMotion: ReduceMotion.System`, and heights measured with `onLayout` (or a transform animated) rather than animated to a hardcoded value, because text can reach 200% [S-L19-016]; pinch zoom stays available [S-L19-028]; light and dark follow the system "as much as possible" [S-L19-067].
  - **Plus an appearance switch in the app:** Kole Jain's Mac app keeps light and dark settings in a settings popover [S-L19-067]. This differs from DC-L10-17 (Apple: no app-only appearance setting). DC-L19-14 already owns this choice for Q-theme-01.
  - **Plus personalization:** when no single layout fits everyone, let people rearrange controls and hide what they don't use [S-L19-020]; the same Mac app lets people choose which side the quick-save panel opens from [S-L19-067]. Mobbin's examples personalize for engagement rather than for access: Moonly fills the home screen's quick-access buttons from onboarding answers [S-L19-111], and Focus Flight lets people pick a map style during onboarding so the app feels like theirs [S-L19-107]. They are good visual samples for this option, but they do not replace any device setting [inferred].
  - **Plus a full high-contrast theme** (7:1): an optional extra mode (DC-L19-17, DC-L01-20).
  - **Plus text-size or density controls in the app** (today's `text-size` and `density` options): no source in this area asks for them. An in-app text-size control repeats the device's own text-size setting on native platforms [inferred]; a compact/roomy switch has no device equivalent, so it stays a genuine in-app option (DC-L03-11) [inferred].
- **Visual effect:** Following the signals: people who turn them on get a solid, bordered, non-moving, larger-text version of the same screen, and nobody else sees a change. In-app controls: a settings popover or panel; more choice for people, more combinations to test.
- **Depends on (upstream):** DC-L19-141 (the floor), Q-plat-01 (macOS has no Dynamic Type, DC-L10-07), Q-theme-01.
- **Affects (downstream):** the motion, transparency and contrast token modes, rem-based spacing, a settings screen or popover, the test matrix (Q-gov-07).
- **Token encoding:** semantic-tier modes `motion: full | reduced`, `transparency: full | reduced`, `contrast: standard | more` (DC-L10-16), written on the web as `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce` and `prefers-contrast: more` [S-L19-020]. In-app switches reuse the engine's existing `[data-theme]` and `[data-density]` overrides; nothing new.
- **Platform notes:** web reads the three media queries [S-L19-020]; React Native reads the system setting per animation [S-L19-016]; macOS follows the system appearance [S-L19-067].
- **Accessibility constraints:** reduced motion keeps opacity and color changes and drops movement; it is never zero. Text scales to 200%; zoom is never disabled.
- **Default + heuristic:** Default: every device signal followed automatically and never asked about; no extra in-app controls unless Q-theme-01 chose a switch or the product serves groups whose needs clash (then personalization). Rule of thumb: if the device already has a switch for it, the product obeys that switch; an in-app control is only for what the device can't express.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-016] [S-L19-020] [S-L19-028] [S-L19-067] [S-L19-107] [S-L19-111]; compared with DC-L10-16, DC-L10-17, DC-L13-14, DC-L19-14, DC-L19-17.
- **Maps to:**
  - Q-aud-04: new ask "Beyond the device's own settings, which controls should people get inside the app?"; `reduced-motion`, and the device parts of `contrast` and `text-size`, become always-on notes instead of options, because the house standards make them musts.
  - Q-aud-04: new option `personalize` (rearrange or hide controls) [S-L19-020]; new default "none beyond the device settings", replacing "text-size + reduced-motion", which are now automatic. Visual sample for `personalize`: a home screen whose quick-access buttons come from onboarding answers [S-L19-111] beside an onboarding step that picks a map style [S-L19-107].
  - Q-aud-04 visual sample: the preview's mode switcher keeps one toggle per device signal, labeled "always followed", so people can see what each one does.
  - Q-motion-10: confirms "all of them" (the list becomes information, not a choice).
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Device signals:* now, three CSS blocks (or three runtime checks) and rem spacing. As it grows, every new translucent, moving or fixed-height component must honor them, which review can check.
  - *Appearance switch:* now, a stored preference and a control. As it grows, extra themes join the same switch (DC-L19-14).
  - *Personalization:* now, a settings model and saved layouts. As it grows, every new control needs a place in the customizable set, and support has more layouts to reason about [inferred].
  - *High-contrast theme:* now, one extra mode. As it grows, every new color needs its 7:1 value.
  - *In-app text size:* now, a duplicate control. As it grows, two text-size settings can fight each other [inferred].
  - *In-app density switch:* now, a compact/comfortable token mode. As it grows, every component needs both densities, with hit areas that never shrink (DC-L03-12).
- **Standards:** STD-accessibility-motion-01, STD-accessibility-motion-02, STD-accessibility-motion-11, STD-accessibility-motion-12, STD-accessibility-motion-13, STD-accessibility-motion-27, STD-visual-details-43, STD-visual-details-64

### DC-L19-143: Mixed input: hover is an extra, press feedback is for everyone
- **Block path:** Foundations > Interaction > Input capability > Hover and press
- **Questions the designer answers:** Will the same screen be used with a finger and a mouse, sometimes on the same device? What happens to anything that only shows on hover? When does a tap show that it landed?
- **Options:**
  - **Mixed input, gated by capability (the house rule for the web):** iPads with trackpads, laptops with touchscreens and phones with a mouse mean touch and mouse are not exclusive. Hover styles live only inside `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`, never behind a user-agent, screen-width or JavaScript touch check [S-L19-028]. Press feedback fires when the finger lands (`:active`, or `pointerdown` in JavaScript, never `click`): scale 0.97 over 100-160ms with ease-out [S-L19-028]. Highlight on touch-down, commit on touch-up, and about 10px of hit padding so a drifting finger keeps its press [S-L19-020].
  - **Touch only (native phone app):** there is no hover, so every hover affordance moves to press, position or nothing, redesigned rather than ported [S-L19-016]. Pressables scale to 0.97 in 100-150ms (the recipe uses 120ms), with `hitSlop` to reach 44pt and `pressRetentionOffset` for drift [S-L19-016] [S-L19-015]. On mobile, a slightly darker gray on press makes it "feel like you're actually pressing into something" [S-L19-051].
  - **Pointer first (desktop):** hover may add hints, such as an arrow fading in on a card that is a link [S-L19-075] or a tooltip on an unclear icon [inferred; the mistakes video's tooltips for two unlabeled nav icons are onboarding pop-ups, not hover hints [S-L19-045]], but only as an extra with a visible or keyboard path too (DC-L13-03: never hover-only for anything essential; DC-L19-55 for card links).
  - **Device sniffing:** ruled out [S-L19-028].
- **Visual effect:** Gated hover: desktops keep hover lifts and tints; phones never show a button stuck in its hover state after a tap [S-L19-028]. Press scale: the whole button, label and icon included, gives under the finger, which reads as physical [S-L19-016]. Touch-only redesign: actions that hid behind hover become visible icons or rows [inferred], or a long-press menu, the mobile equivalent of the right click [S-L19-053].
- **Depends on (upstream):** Q-plat-01, Q-plat-02 (devices), DC-L19-141.
- **Affects (downstream):** every interactive component's state rules, tooltips (need a non-hover trigger), whole-card links, `size.target.*`, Q-state-04.
- **Token encoding:** existing `size.target.pointer` (24) and `size.target.touch` (44 or 48), $type dimension. Press feedback as motion tokens, for example `motion.press.scale` ($type number, 0.97) and `motion.press.duration` ($type duration, 100ms) [inferred names]. Hover gating is an output rule of the CSS export, not a token.
- **Platform notes:** web: remove the tap highlight globally only together with an `:active` state on every tappable, and put `touch-action: manipulation` on tappables to remove the tap delay [S-L19-028]. React Native: Pressable with a CSS transition [S-L19-016]. Android ripple only in a Material-styled app (DC-L19-147).
- **Accessibility constraints:** WCAG 1.4.13 for content shown on hover; 2.5.8 targets; whatever hover reveals must also be reachable by keyboard focus [inferred].
- **Default + heuristic:** Default for Q-plat-03: touch + pointer + keyboard, treated as possibly on the same device, on every web surface; native phone apps are touch plus the operating system's keyboard and switch access [inferred]. Rule of thumb: design the touch version first; hover can only add, never hold something people need.
- **Evidence:** [S-L19-015] [S-L19-016] [S-L19-020] [S-L19-028] [S-L19-045] [S-L19-051] [S-L19-053] [S-L19-075]; compared with DC-L10-15, DC-L14-06, DC-L03-12, DC-L13-03, DC-L19-93, DC-L19-103.
- **Maps to:**
  - Q-plat-03: new heuristic and Use/avoid line "hover never carries anything essential; gate it by capability, never by device" [S-L19-028]; the default text becomes "touch + pointer + keyboard, possibly on the same device" (confirms the current default set).
  - Q-plat-03 visual sample: a phone screen where a tapped button stays in its hover state, beside the gated version, and a button scaling to 0.97 as the finger lands [S-L19-028].
  - Q-state-04: no separate change here. Its current default (all eight states, overlays for hover and press) gains the press scale from DC-L19-93 and the gated hover from DC-L19-103; this card only adds that the same device may be used by finger and mouse, which is what the `per-input` option describes.
  - Engine: the preview's ungated `:hover` rules are already recorded as a conflict under STD-accessibility-motion-15; no new note.
- **Impact now / as it grows:**
  - *Mixed input:* now, one media query around every hover rule and an `:active` rule per control. As it grows, new devices (touch laptops, tablets with keyboards) just work, because nothing depends on the device name.
  - *Touch only:* now, hover ideas must be redesigned, not copied. As it grows, a later web or desktop version adds hover as an extra without changing the base.
  - *Pointer first:* now, richer hover hints. As it grows, every hover hint needs a touch and keyboard twin, or it becomes a trap when touch use grows.
  - *Device sniffing:* now, it seems to work on the designer's devices. As it grows, it breaks on each new mixed-input device.
- **Standards:** STD-mobile-touch-02, STD-mobile-touch-03, STD-mobile-touch-05, STD-mobile-touch-06, STD-mobile-touch-08, STD-mobile-touch-09, STD-mobile-touch-30, STD-accessibility-motion-15, STD-components-toasts-drawers-72

### DC-L19-144: Web product on phones: installed-app feel or scrolling document
- **Block path:** Platforms > Web > Mobile web posture
- **Questions the designer answers:** When people open the web product on a phone, should it feel like an installed app or like a page? Will people add it to their home screen? Does a marketing site sit next to the app?
- **Options:**
